title: Rebuilding a portfolio site with Hugo

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A diagram that's cropped loses its meaning. Cut off the axes of a surface plot or the labels of an architecture diagram and the reader is left guessing.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That feels like a small detail to build a whole redesign around.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's one of many. Antoine rebuilt his Hugo portfolio so the CV, the articles and the repository notes share one visual identity, while each kind of page keeps a layout that suits its reading. A slate-blue background, pale paper surface, teal for links and actions, and Fraunces for the titles.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. The CV leads with the name, portrait and PDF button. An article needs a comfortable reading column. A project reference needs room for commands, API tables and diagrams. On a narrow screen, navigation wraps and long code scrolls inside its own block.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the technical side? He changed themes, didn't he?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He moved from HBTheme to Paper and now owns the overrides in his own templates. That means one template fix applies across all articles. The header groups the content kind, date, reading time and topic badges, and longer articles get a collapsible contents list.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What about the French and English versions?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: They're paired with a translation key, and the language switcher sits in the site header. He also avoids repeating a translation link in each introduction, because that paragraph should introduce the subject.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Mermaid diagrams now have zoom, fit, full size, fullscreen and SVG export. They start fitted to the space, so you can inspect one label without scrolling sideways.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Repository skills, yes. Small rule sets that keep recurring edits consistent: one for the CV pages, one for the Hugo templates and bilingual bundles, one for project notes and the evidence behind technical claims. Antoine adds that a rule can't tell whether an image belongs to the project or whether a label is legible, so everything still gets reviewed.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How does he check a page before publishing?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He builds locally, then checks light and dark mode, small and wide screens, language links, images and controls. Reduced-motion settings have to leave all content reachable too.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A build passing isn't enough, then.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. The full write-up has the diagram of the whole flow from git to the published static site.
